summary: This document adds an NNTP extension for authentication, letting a client pick a method, run an authentication exchange and optionally set up a security layer. It formalizes AUTHINFO USER/PASS from RFC 2980, deprecates two older methods, and defines a SASL profile for NNTP.

plainLanguage.summary: News servers have traditionally served anyone who connects. This RFC adds an authentication extension to NNTP so a server can tell who is asking. It formalizes the widely used AUTHINFO USER and PASS commands, and defines AUTHINFO SASL, which lets a client use the same authentication mechanisms as other protocols, with the option of setting up an encrypted layer for the rest of the session.

subtitle: An NNTP extension that lets a client authenticate before it reads or posts to a news server.

tldr.problem: News servers have traditionally given open access to anyone who connects, but an operator may need to control resource use, identify people who abuse the POST command, or keep some newsgroups local.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three commands, AUTHINFO USER, AUTHINFO PASS and AUTHINFO SASL, advertised through a new AUTHINFO capability. AUTHINFO SASL runs the standard SASL exchange, with base64 challenges and responses, and can agree a security layer for the rest of the session.
tldr.outcome: The widely used but weak USER and PASS commands are formalized for use only with a strong encryption layer, while AUTHINFO GENERIC is deprecated in favour of SASL, so news servers can use the same mechanisms as SMTP, POP and IMAP. Implementations must support the DIGEST-MD5 mechanism.

facts.label: New commands
facts.value: AUTHINFO USER, AUTHINFO PASS, AUTHINFO SASL

facts.label: Command length
facts.value: AUTHINFO SASL may exceed 512 octets to carry the largest initial response

today: RFC 4643 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, though it updates RFC 2980 by formalizing the AUTHINFO USER and PASS commands and deprecating AUTHINFO GENERIC. It remains the authentication extension for NNTP.

sections.title: Why News Needs Authentication
sections.content:
Although NNTP has traditionally been used to provide public access to newsgroups, authentication is often useful for several purposes: to control resource consumption, to allow abusers of the POST command to be identified, and to restrict access to 'local' newsgroups.

The ad-hoc AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS commands provide a very weak authentication mechanism in widespread use by the installed base. Due to their ubiquity they are formalized in this specification, but, because of their insecurity, only for use in combination with appropriate security layers.

The ad hoc AUTHINFO GENERIC command provided an NNTP-specific equivalent of the generic SASL facility, but it was much less ubiquitous. This document deprecates AUTHINFO GENERIC in favor of an AUTHINFO SASL replacement, so that NNTP can benefit from authentication mechanisms developed for other SASL-enabled application protocols, including SMTP, POP, IMAP, LDAP and BEEP.

The extension is used to authenticate a user. Authorization is a matter of site policy, not network protocol, and is therefore not discussed in the document: the server determines authorization in whatever manner its implementation and the site administrator define.
sections.plainLanguage: NNTP is usually used to give public access to newsgroups, but authentication is often useful: to control resource use, to identify people who abuse the POST command, and to restrict access to local newsgroups. The AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS commands have been in wide use but are weak, so this RFC formalizes them for use only with a proper security layer. The older AUTHINFO GENERIC command is deprecated in favour of AUTHINFO SASL, so that news servers can use the same authentication mechanisms as SMTP, POP, IMAP, LDAP and BEEP.

sections.title: Advertising the Extension and Starting the Exchange
sections.content:
A server MUST implement at least one of the AUTHINFO USER or AUTHINFO SASL commands in order to advertise the 'AUTHINFO' capability label in response to the CAPABILITIES command. This capability MUST NOT be advertised after successful authentication, and it MAY be advertised both before and after any use of the MODE READER command, with the same semantics.

The AUTHINFO capability label contains an argument list detailing which authentication commands are available. The 'USER' argument indicates that AUTHINFO USER and PASS are supported, and it MUST NOT be advertised, and those commands SHOULD NOT be provided, unless a strong encryption layer such as TLS is in use or backward compatibility dictates otherwise. The 'SASL' argument indicates that AUTHINFO SASL is supported, and if the server advertises it, then it MUST also advertise the 'SASL' capability in response to CAPABILITIES, followed by a whitespace-separated list of available SASL mechanism names. The server MAY list the AUTHINFO capability with no arguments, which indicates that it complies with the specification and does not permit any authentication commands in its current state, and in that case the client MUST NOT attempt to use any AUTHINFO command. Future extensions may add arguments, and unrecognized arguments MUST be ignored by the client.

Because the AUTHINFO command is related to security, cached results of CAPABILITIES from a previous session MUST NOT be relied on, although a client MAY use such cached results in order to detect active down-negotiation attacks.

An NNTP server responds to a client command with a 480 response to indicate that the client MUST authenticate and authorize in order to use that command or access the indicated resource, and a client MAY therefore use an AUTHINFO command after receiving a 480 response. A client intending to use AUTHINFO SHOULD issue the CAPABILITIES command first to learn the available commands and mechanisms. If the server advertises the AUTHINFO capability, a client MAY attempt the first step of authentication at any time during a session to acquire additional privileges without having received a 480 response, and servers SHOULD accept such unsolicited requests. A server MUST NOT under any circumstances reply to an AUTHINFO command with a 480 response, and a client MUST NOT continue with any step of authentication beyond the first unless the response code indicates that the exchange is welcomed.

After a successful authentication the client MUST NOT issue another AUTHINFO command in the same session, a server MUST NOT return the AUTHINFO capability in response to CAPABILITIES and MUST reject any subsequent AUTHINFO commands with a 502 response, and the client MUST NOT issue a MODE READER command after authentication while the server MUST NOT advertise the MODE-READER capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The server advertises the extension in its CAPABILITIES list with the label AUTHINFO. The label can carry the argument USER, the argument SASL, or no arguments at all, which means the server complies with the specification but currently permits no authentication. If SASL is advertised, the server must also list the SASL capability with the mechanism names it supports. A client that wants to authenticate should ask for the capabilities first, and it can also authenticate at any time, not only after the server refuses a command with a 480. Once authentication has succeeded, the AUTHINFO capability must no longer be advertised and any further AUTHINFO command must be rejected with a 502.

sections.title: The AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS Commands
sections.content:
These commands MUST NOT be pipelined. The syntax is AUTHINFO USER username and AUTHINFO PASS password, and the responses are 281 Authentication accepted, 381 Password required, 481 Authentication failed or rejected, 482 Authentication commands issued out of sequence and 502 Command unavailable. The 381 code is only valid for AUTHINFO USER, and unlike traditional 3xx codes, which indicate that the client may continue the current command, the legacy 381 code means that the AUTHINFO PASS command must be used to complete the authentication exchange. The server MUST NOT return 480 in response to AUTHINFO USER or PASS.

The two commands present clear text credentials to the server. The credentials consist of a username, or a username plus a password; the distinction is that a password is expected to be kept secret whereas a username is not. If the server requires only a username, it MUST NOT give a 381 response to AUTHINFO USER and MUST give a 482 response to AUTHINFO PASS. If it requires both, the username MUST be sent before the password, and the server will need to cache the username until the password is received. The server MUST return a 381 response to AUTHINFO USER, MUST return a 482 response to AUTHINFO PASS if there is no cached username, MUST use the argument of the most recent AUTHINFO USER for authentication, and MUST NOT return a 381 response to AUTHINFO PASS.

A compliant implementation MUST NOT implement AUTHINFO PASS without also implementing support for TLS. Use of the command without an active strong encryption layer is deprecated, as it exposes the user's password to all parties on the network between the client and the server. Any implementation SHOULD be configurable to disable it whenever a strong encryption layer is not active, and that configuration SHOULD be the default. The server uses the 483 response code to indicate that the datastream is insufficiently secure for the command being attempted.

A server MAY, but is not required to, allow white space characters in usernames and passwords, and a client SHOULD scan the username and password for white space and warn the user of the likelihood of problems. The SASL PLAIN mechanism is recommended as an alternative, as it does not suffer from these issues. Historically the username is not canonicalized in any way, and servers MAY use the SASLprep profile of the StringPrep algorithm to prepare usernames for comparison, though doing so may cause interoperability problems with legacy implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTHINFO USER sends a user name and AUTHINFO PASS sends a password in the clear. The server answers 281 when the credentials are accepted, 381 when it wants a password after a user name, 481 when the credentials are refused, and 482 when the commands arrive in the wrong order. A compliant implementation must not offer AUTHINFO PASS without also supporting TLS, because the password is exposed to everyone on the path. A server that needs a stronger layer answers 483 instead.

sections.title: The AUTHINFO SASL Command
sections.content:
This section defines a formal profile of SASL. The use of AUTHINFO GENERIC as a way to perform SASL authentication is deprecated in favor of AUTHINFO SASL, and a server SHOULD NOT advertise AUTHINFO GENERIC in the list of capabilities returned by CAPABILITIES. The command MUST NOT be pipelined, and its syntax is AUTHINFO SASL mechanism [initial-response]. It MAY exceed 512 octets: the maximum length is increased to whatever can accommodate the largest encoded initial response possible for any of the SASL mechanisms supported by the implementation.

The responses are 281 Authentication accepted, 283 challenge Authentication accepted with success data, 383 challenge Continue with SASL exchange, 481 Authentication failed or rejected, 482 SASL protocol error and 502 Command unavailable. The 283 and 383 responses MAY also exceed 512 octets. If the requested mechanism is invalid, the server rejects the command with a 503 reply, and if it requires an encryption layer, with a 483 reply. The service name specified by this profile of SASL is 'nntp'.

The exchange consists of a series of server challenges and client responses specific to the chosen mechanism. A server challenge is sent as a 383 reply with a single argument containing the base64-encoded string supplied by the mechanism; a zero-length challenge MUST be sent as a single equals sign. A client response is a line containing a base64-encoded string, and a zero-length response MUST be sent as a single equals sign. If the client wishes to cancel the exchange, it issues a line with a single asterisk, and the server MUST reject the command by sending a 481 reply. Servers and clients MUST reject any character not explicitly allowed by the base64 alphabet, and MUST reject any sequence that contains the pad character anywhere other than at the end.

The optional initial response saves a round trip with mechanisms that support one. If it is omitted and the mechanism requires an initial response, the server proceeds as defined in the SASL specification. If the client uses an initial response with a mechanism that does not support one, the server MUST reject the command with a 482 reply. If the server cannot base64 decode a client response it MUST reject the command with a 504 reply.

Should the client complete the exchange successfully, the server issues a 281 reply, or a 283 reply with the base64-encoded additional data if the mechanism returned any. If a security layer is negotiated during the exchange, it takes effect for the client on the octet immediately following the CRLF that concludes the last client response, and for the server immediately following the CRLF of its success reply. When the security layer takes effect, the NNTP protocol is reset to the state immediately after the initial greeting response, with the exception that the effects of an earlier MODE READER command are not reversed, and any knowledge obtained from the other party that was not obtained from the SASL negotiation itself is discarded. When both TLS and SASL security layers are in effect, the TLS encoding MUST be applied after the SASL encoding.

To ensure interoperability, client and server implementations MUST implement the DIGEST-MD5 SASL mechanism. If both AUTHINFO USER/PASS and AUTHINFO SASL are implemented, the SASL PLAIN mechanism SHOULD also be implemented, as the functionality of DIGEST-MD5 is insufficient for some environments, such as a server that has to pass the plaintext password to an external authentication service.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTHINFO SASL names a mechanism and can carry an initial response, both in base64. The server answers 383 with a challenge, the client replies with a base64 line, and the exchange continues until the server answers 281 or 283. A client that wants to stop sends a single asterisk and gets a 481 back. A zero-length value is written as a single equals sign. If the mechanism succeeds and returns extra data, the server sends 283 with that data. The exchange can also agree a security layer, which takes effect immediately after the final line and resets the protocol state.

sections.title: The Grammar of the Extension
sections.content:
The formal syntax of the AUTHINFO extension is given in ABNF, extending the syntax in Section 9 of the NNTP base specification. The command production is extended with three alternatives: authinfo-sasl-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "SASL" WS mechanism [WS initial-response], authinfo-user-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "USER" WS username and authinfo-pass-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "PASS" WS password, where the initial response is a base64 value and the username and password are one or more user-pass characters. A server implementation MAY parse AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS specially so as to allow white space inside the username or password, accepting the additional syntax, although that can make the grammar ambiguous if the name begins or ends with white space.

The command-continuation production is extended with authinfo-sasl-383-continuation = ("*" / base64-opt) CRLF. The initial-response-content production is extended with response-283-content = "283" SP base64 and response-383-content = "383" SP base64-opt. The capability-entry production is extended with authinfo-capability = "AUTHINFO" *(WS authinfo-variant), where a variant is USER or SASL, and sasl-capability = "SASL" 1*(WS mechanism). The mechanism name is one to twenty characters drawn from upper case letters, digits, hyphen and underscore.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives the grammar of the new commands and responses. The three commands are AUTHINFO SASL with an optional initial response, AUTHINFO USER and AUTHINFO PASS. A continuation line is either a single asterisk or a base64 value. The two new responses are 283 with a base64 argument and 383 with an optional base64 argument, and the capability entries are AUTHINFO with zero or more arguments and SASL followed by a list of mechanism names.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Logging
sections.content:
Security issues are discussed throughout the memo. In general, the security considerations of SASL and any implemented SASL mechanisms apply here, and this extension is not intended to cure the security considerations described in Section 12 of the NNTP specification.

Before the SASL negotiation has begun, any protocol interactions may have been performed in the clear and may have been modified by an active attacker. For this reason, clients and servers MUST discard any sensitive knowledge obtained prior to the start of the SASL negotiation upon the establishment of a security layer, the CAPABILITIES command SHOULD be re-issued upon the establishment of a security layer, and other protocol state SHOULD be re-negotiated as well.

Servers MAY implement a policy whereby the connection is dropped after a number of failed authentication attempts, and if they do so they SHOULD NOT drop the connection until at least three attempts have failed. Implementations MUST support a configuration where authentication mechanisms that are vulnerable to passive eavesdropping attacks, such as AUTHINFO USER/PASS and SASL PLAIN, are not advertised or used without the presence of an external security layer such as TLS, and this configuration SHOULD be the default. When multiple authentication mechanisms are permitted by both client and server, an active attacker can cause a down-negotiation to the weakest mechanism, so both clients and servers SHOULD be configurable to forbid the use of weak mechanisms.

Separately, the RFC recommends that once authenticated, the authorization identity presented in the AUTHINFO exchange SHOULD be included in an audit trail associating the identity with any articles supplied during a POST operation, and that this configuration SHOULD be the default. This may be accomplished, for example, by inserting headers in the posted articles or by a server logging mechanism. The server MAY provide a facility for disabling the procedure, as some users or administrators may consider it a violation of privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything said before the SASL negotiation starts may have been read or altered on the way, so once an encrypted layer is in place both sides must throw away what they learned earlier and re-issue the capability list. A server may drop the connection after several failed attempts, but not before three. Implementations must be able to switch off the mechanisms that expose passwords, such as AUTHINFO USER/PASS and SASL PLAIN, unless an external layer such as TLS is present, and that should be the default. When several mechanisms are allowed, an attacker can try to force the weakest one, so both ends should be able to refuse weak mechanisms. The RFC also recommends recording the identity of an authenticated user in articles they post, so that abuse can be traced.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the SASL/GSSAPI service name 'nntp', which refers to authenticated use of the Usenet news service when it is provided via the NNTP protocol. The published specification is this document, the contact for further information is the authors of this document, and the change controller is the IESG.

The extension is registered formally as required for the IANA registry of NNTP extensions. It provides an extensible mechanism for NNTP authentication via a variety of methods, with the capability label 'AUTHINFO' and two possible optional arguments, 'USER' and 'SASL', indicating which variants of the AUTHINFO command are supported. It also provides the 'SASL' capability label, whose arguments list the available SASL mechanisms.

The extension defines three new commands, AUTHINFO USER, AUTHINFO PASS and AUTHINFO SASL, and does not associate any new responses with pre-existing NNTP commands. It defines two new responses, 283 and 383, whose lengths may exceed 512 octets. The extension does not alter pipelining, but AUTHINFO commands cannot be pipelined. It does not cause any pre-existing command to produce a 401, 480 or 483 response, and it is unaffected by any use of the MODE READER command, although MODE READER MUST NOT be used in the same session following successful authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA registered the SASL service name nntp for authenticated use of the Usenet service over NNTP. The extension itself is registered with the capability label AUTHINFO, the two optional arguments USER and SASL, and the separate SASL capability label. Two new response codes, 283 and 383, are defined, and both may be longer than the usual 512 octets.

viz.caption: THE GRAMMAR OF THE NEW COMMANDS AND RESPONSES

data.title: ABNF from section 3
data.code:
command =/ authinfo-sasl-command /
         authinfo-user-command /
         authinfo-pass-command

authinfo-sasl-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "SASL" WS mechanism
         [WS initial-response]
authinfo-user-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "USER" WS username
authinfo-pass-command = "AUTHINFO" WS "PASS" WS password

initial-response = base64-opt
username = 1*user-pass-char
password = 1*user-pass-char
user-pass-char = B-CHAR

command-continuation =/ authinfo-sasl-383-continuation
authinfo-sasl-383-continuation = ("*" / base64-opt) CRLF

initial-response-content =/ response-283-content /
         response-383-content
response-283-content = "283" SP base64
response-383-content = "383" SP base64-opt

capability-entry =/ authinfo-capability /
         sasl-capability
authinfo-capability = "AUTHINFO" *(WS authinfo-variant)
authinfo-variant = "USER" / "SASL"
sasl-capability = "SASL" 1*(WS mechanism)

viz.caption: THE RESPONSE CODES THE EXTENSION DEFINES

items.label: Authentication accepted
items.desc: Generated by AUTHINFO USER, PASS and SASL.

items.label: Accepted with success data
items.desc: One base64 argument. Generated by AUTHINFO SASL.

items.label: Password required
items.desc: Generated by AUTHINFO USER. A legacy code that does not follow the usual 3xx meaning.

items.label: Continue the SASL exchange
items.desc: One base64 argument holding the server challenge.

items.label: Authentication failed
items.desc: The credentials were refused, or the client cancelled the exchange.

items.label: Out of sequence
items.desc: The commands came in the wrong order, or there was a SASL protocol error.

items.label: Command unavailable
items.desc: Returned when a further AUTHINFO command arrives after a successful authentication.
